sentences: We formulate benchmark construction as constrained compilation, in which the benchmark specification is progressively derived from evaluation requirements, heterogeneous annotations, and medical knowledge.

Based on this formulation, we introduce MedBenchAgent, a multi-agent framework with a Benchmark Intermediate Representation (BIR) that encodes task definitions, evidence mappings, evaluation protocols, and item specifications across construction stages.
MedBenchAgent separates planning, which derives and verifies the specification, from instantiation, which constructs and audits items under the locked specification.

MedBenchAgent achieves a Task-Space F1 of 90.9%, outperforming direct task induction (79.2–80.0%) and prior-guided induction (85.1%); 994 of 1,000 sampled items from correctly identified tasks pass human audit.
We further demonstrate portability to a specialized medical domain and evaluate twelve VLMs, revealing task- and setting-specific variation obscured by aggregate scores.
These results establish constrained compilation as a scalable and auditable framework for medical VLM benchmark construction beyond question generation.
We address this challenge with MedBenchAgent, a multi-agent framework for systematic medical VLM benchmark construction.

We cast benchmark construction as constrained compilation, in which the benchmark specification is progressively established from an intended evaluation scope, heterogeneous source annotations, and medical knowledge, with each confirmed decision narrowing the space of subsequent construction.

To make these constraints explicit and preserve them across stages, we introduce a Benchmark Intermediate Representation (BIR) that records the evaluation scope, task hierarchy, annotation evidence mappings, evaluation protocols, sample allocations, and item-construction specifications.
In construction analysis, MedBenchAgent achieves a Task-Space F1 of 90.9%, compared with 79.2–80.0% for direct task induction and 85.1% when the same task prior is provided to the direct model.

MedBenchAgent operationalizes this formulation through a staged multi-agent workflow for medical benchmark construction: 1) planning resolves and verifies the specification against dataset annotations and medical references before locking the BIR; and 2) instantiation constructs and audits evaluation items under this fixed specification.

In this way, MedBenchAgent extends automation from predefined medical scopes or question structures to benchmark specification itself, while preserving the annotation and medical constraints required for reliable construction.

Model evaluation reveals substantial variation across tasks, imaging settings, and evaluation metrics that aggregate scores can obscure, reinforcing fine-grained benchmark specification as an important component of medical VLM evaluation.

Overall, this work makes three contributions: (1) Conceptually, we model the construction of medical VLM benchmarks and formulate it as constrained compilation; (2) Methodologically, we introduce a multi-agent MedBenchAgent framework and its Benchmark Intermediate Representation (BIR); and (3) Empirically, we derive insights into both the benchmark-construction process and medical VLM evaluation, while providing reusable benchmark artifacts.

We introduced MedBenchAgent, a multi-agent framework that treats medical VLM benchmark construction as constrained compilation and makes benchmark specification an explicit, auditable object of construction.

Through the Benchmark Intermediate Representation (BIR), MedBenchAgent separates specification planning from downstream item instantiation, allowing construction decisions to be evaluated stage by stage rather than only through the final benchmark.

Our analyses identify open-ended task-space specification as the primary source of construction uncertainty, while annotation-evidence mapping and item instantiation become substantially more reliable once benchmark semantics are fixed.
Evaluation of the resulting benchmark further reveals task-, metric-, and imaging-dependent variation across VLMs that aggregate scores can obscure.

Together with the cross-domain instantiation under a specialized medical setting, these results show that constrained, multi-agent benchmark construction can support both scalable medical VLM evaluation and systematic study of the benchmark-construction process itself.
